before.title: Weight-one block decomposition pattern
before.statement: Let $e\ge2$, let $\gamma$ be an $e$-core of $m$, and put $n=m+e$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). There are exactly $e$ partitions $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_e$ of $n$ with $e$-core $\gamma$; list them in dominance order, $\lambda_1\rhd\lambda_2\rhd\cdots\rhd\lambda_e$. In the source's (Murphy/dual-Specht) normalisation the Weyl modules and simple modules of this block satisfy $W^{\lambda_e}=L^{\lambda_e}$ and $[W^{\lambda_k}]=[L^{\lambda_k}]+[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]$ for $1\le k<e$, so the decomposition matrix is the $e\times e$ bidiagonal matrix with rows and columns $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_e$; and exactly $\lambda_1$ is not $e$-restricted while $\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_e$ are. Under the Schur functor ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]) the corresponding Murphy Specht classes are $[S^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}]$, $[S^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}]+[D^{\lambda_{k+1}}_{\mathrm M}]$ for $2\le k<e$ and $[S^{\lambda_e}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_e}_{\mathrm M}]$, with $D^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}=0$; conjugating partitions and applying the same $\theta$ pullback to both modules ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]) gives the corresponding decomposition matrix for the page's Dipper-James Specht modules in $e$-regular labels.
before.strategy: The abacus of [[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]] shows that the partitions of $n=m+e$ with $e$-core $\gamma$ are obtained from $\gamma$ by moving one bead up one row on one runner, so there are exactly $e$ of them; ordered by dominance they are $\lambda_1\rhd\cdots\rhd\lambda_e$, with $\lambda_e$ the one whose bead has the lowest target position and $\lambda_1$ the one obtained by adjoining all $e$ boxes to the first row. For each $k$ the Jantzen sum formula of [[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]] evaluates in this weight-one configuration to $\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda_k}_F(i)]\sim\sum_{j>k}(-1)^{j-k+1}[W^{\lambda_j}_F]$, because the only nonzero hook valuations are the consecutive ones; the resulting triangular system, with the simple modules detected through [[lem-virtual-weyl-combinations-detect-q-schur-block-separation]] and the block classification, has the unique solution $[W^{\lambda_k}]=[L^{\lambda_k}]+[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]$ for $k<e$ and $W^{\lambda_e}=L^{\lambda_e}$. The $e$-restricted pattern follows from $D^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}=0$, which is exactly the non-$e$-restricted vanishing of the cell head, together with $F(W^{\lambda_1})=F(L^{\lambda_2})$ and the Schur-functor dictionary; the Dipper-James translation is the signed conjugate-cell dictionary with the same $\theta$ pullback on every Hecke module of the Specht-module definition. This is Mathas, Proposition 5.38 with its printed Jantzen computation, printed pp. 61-63; the numeric pattern is worked out again in this pair's examples companion. No choice principle is used.

after.title: The weight-one block decomposition pattern
after.statement:
Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e\ge2$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), let $\gamma$ be an $e$-core of $m$, and put $n=m+e$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). There are exactly $e$ partitions $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_e$ of $n$ with $e$-core $\gamma$; list them in dominance order, $\lambda_1\rhd\lambda_2\rhd\cdots\rhd\lambda_e$. In the source's (Murphy) normalisation the Weyl modules and simple modules of this weight-one class satisfy $W^{\lambda_e}=L^{\lambda_e}$ and $$[W^{\lambda_k}]=[L^{\lambda_k}]+[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]\qquad(1\le k<e),$$ so the decomposition matrix of the class is the $e\times e$ bidiagonal matrix with rows and columns $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_e$. Moreover exactly $\lambda_1$ is not $e$-restricted, while $\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_e$ are. Under the Schur functor ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]) the corresponding Murphy Specht classes are $$[S^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}],\qquad [S^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}]+[D^{\lambda_{k+1}}_{\mathrm M}]\ (2\le k<e),\qquad [S^{\lambda_e}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_e}_{\mathrm M}],$$ with $D^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}=0$; conjugating partitions and applying the same $\theta$ pullback to both modules ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]) gives the corresponding decomposition matrix for the page's Dipper-James Specht modules in $e$-regular labels.

No choice principle is used.
after.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e\ge2$, an $e$-core $\gamma$ of $m$, the integer $n=m+e$, and the Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}_F$ of $S_F(d,n)$ for $\lambda\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts, where $d\ge n$.

[F1] Each Weyl module has simple head $L^{\lambda}$ of multiplicity one, the decomposition matrix is dominance-unitriangular, and all simple modules are obtained this way ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). In a finite-dimensional module, a simple head implies indecomposability: any nonzero direct summand has a nonzero head, so two nonzero summands would give a nonsimple head.

[F2] The corrected balanced Jantzen formula sums positive filtration **submodules**, not their successive quotients: $$\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda}_F(i)]=\sum_{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda],\ b<c}\bigl(\nu_\pi([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q})-\nu_\pi([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q})\bigr)[W^{\beta+h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_b-h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_c}_F].$$ Here $\beta_b=\lambda'_b+N-b$ for a fixed sufficiently long conjugate beta sequence, and the right hand symbols are alternating symbols: sort strictly decreasing, attach the sorting sign, and vanish on repeated or negative entries. The equal transfer preserves total size. Moreover $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$. This is the balanced hook-ratio formula required from [[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]] and [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. Its source arithmetic must be repaired before binding: the manuscript's displayed beta indices are inconsistent, while its worked Example 5.28 determines the balanced transfer.

[F3] Core-quotient and abacus theory: a weight-one partition is obtained from a packed core abacus by moving the bottom bead of one runner down one place. The bead move removes/adds a rim $e$-hook, and distinct runners give distinct partitions ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]], [[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). Restricted means $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ for every $i$ ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]).

[F4] The exact Schur functor sends $W^{\lambda}$ to $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ and $L^{\lambda}$ to $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$, whose nonzero labels are precisely the restricted partitions. The ordinary Specht dictionary uses conjugation and the same $\theta$ pullback on every module ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]], [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Enumeration and ordering. Choose a conjugate core beta set long enough that every runner contains a bead, and list its bottom beads $x_1<\cdots<x_e$. Each runner is packed, so replacing $x_k$ by $x_k+e$ gives precisely the $e$ weight-one partitions, denoted $\lambda_k$. For $j>k$, moving $x_j$ instead of $x_k$ gives the more dominant conjugate partition: comparing the sorted bead lists, each partial sum increases when the move starts at the larger bead. Conjugation reverses dominance, hence $\lambda_1\rhd\cdots\rhd\lambda_e$. The largest original partition is $(\gamma_1+e,\gamma_2,\ldots)$, since its added horizontal first-row strip dominates every other placement. [F3, construct, algebra]

1.2 Choose a lift with valuation one. If $q\ne1$, its finite quantum characteristic $e$ is its multiplicative order, and is prime to the field characteristic; use $R=F[X]_{(X-q)}$ and $\hat q=X$. The derivative of $X^e-1$ at $q$ is $eq^{e-1}\ne0$, so $\nu([e]_X)=1$; also $\nu([h]_X)=0$ when $e\nmid h$. If $q=1$, then $\operatorname{char}F=p=e$. First work over $\mathbb F_p$ with $R=\mathbb Z_{(p)}$, $\hat q=1$, giving $\nu([e]_1)=\nu(p)=1$ and $\nu([h]_1)=0$ for $p\nmid h$, and then extend scalars to $F$. This extension preserves the decomposition multiplicities because the q-Schur simple modules are absolutely irreducible and its integral Weyl modules commute with scalar extension. In both cases the generic factorial is nonzero and [F2] applies. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Restriction. If $\lambda$ is not restricted, some $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}\ge e$, so removing the last $e$ boxes of row $i$ leaves a partition. Its size is $|\gamma|$ and its core is $\gamma$, so it equals $\gamma$. Thus $\lambda$ is obtained by adding $e$ boxes to row $i$ of $\gamma$. An $e$-core has $\gamma_r-\gamma_{r+1}<e$ for every $r$, since otherwise it has a removable horizontal $e$-strip. Consequently $i>1$ is impossible: the partition inequality $\gamma_{i-1}\ge\gamma_i+e$ would contradict this core property. Therefore the only nonrestricted member is $\lambda_1=(\gamma_1+e,\gamma_2,\ldots)$; it is indeed nonrestricted because its first-row difference is at least $e$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Evaluate the balanced formula. A nonzero coefficient involves a hook of length divisible by $e$. A weight-one abacus has exactly one bead-gap pair of equal residue with the gap below the bead: $x_k+e$ and $x_k$; thus its only $e$-divisible hook has length $e$. Any surviving term in [F2] replaces two bead values, and its new runner counts equal the old ones: either $e$ divides the transfer $h_{ac}$, leaving residues fixed, or $e$ divides $h_{ab}=h_{ac}+\beta_b-\beta_c$, exchanging their residues. Hence its sorted symbol is one of the $\lambda_j$. For $j>k$, the distinct bead sets of $\lambda_k$ and $\lambda_j$ differ exactly by replacing $x_k+e,x_j$ with $x_k,x_j+e$. There is exactly one balanced transfer yielding this change: if $x_j<x_k+e$, its two hook lengths are $h_{ab}=e$, $h_{ac}=x_j-x_k$; if $x_j>x_k+e$, they are $h_{ab}=x_j-x_k$, $h_{ac}=e$. The difference $x_j-x_k$ is not divisible by $e$ since bottom beads are on distinct runners. Thus the respective unsigned coefficients are $+1$ and $-1$ by step 1.2. Sorting gives in either case the signed coefficient $(-1)^{j-k+1}$: in the packed core set, exactly one bead from each runner with bottom bead $>x_r$ lies between $x_r$ and $x_r+e$, so moving $x_r$ crosses $e-r$ beads; the relative sorting parity for the two moves, together with their opposite orientation, is $(-1)^{(e-j)-(e-k)+1}$. There are no other terms and no repeated contributions: the two lost and two gained bead values determine the pair and transfer uniquely. Therefore $\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda_k}(i)]=\sum_{j>k}(-1)^{j-k+1}[W^{\lambda_j}]$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Descending induction and the matrix. For $k=e$, step 2.2 gives zero on the left; all summands are actual submodule classes with nonnegative simple multiplicities, so $W^{\lambda_e}(1)=0$ and $W^{\lambda_e}=L^{\lambda_e}$. Suppose the stated rows are known for $j>k$. Substitution into step 2.2 telescopes to $\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda_k}(i)]=[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]$. Since $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$ and each later term is a submodule of $W(1)$, positivity shows $W(1)\cong L^{\lambda_{k+1}}$ and $W(i)=0$ for $i\ge2$. The head quotient is $L^{\lambda_k}$, giving $[W^{\lambda_k}]=[L^{\lambda_k}]+[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]$. Notice that the identity $[W]=[L]+\sum_{i>0}[W(i)]$ is used only after proving all later filtration submodules vanish; it is false for a general Jantzen filtration. Reading simple multiplicities yields the complete $e\times e$ bidiagonal matrix. [F1, F2, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Specht rows. Apply the exact functor of [F4] to step 3.1 and use step 2.1: $D^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}=0$, while the other $D^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}$ are the nonzero simples. This gives exactly the three displayed Murphy Specht class identities, hence the full $e\times(e-1)$ Murphy matrix. Conjugation sends the core to $\gamma'$ and the restricted simple labels to regular ones, and the same $\theta$ pullback applied to every module preserves all composition multiplicities. Thus the ordinary Specht matrix has the same entries under the accepted conjugate/sign label dictionary. [F4, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

before.title: The Schur functor compares first-level branching with Hecke restriction
before.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^\times$, $\ell$ the quantum characteristic of $q$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) and
$n\ge r$. Let $S(n,r)$ be the type-A q-Schur algebra with the idempotent $e$
of the weight $(1^r)$, so that $eS(n,r)e\cong H(r)$, and let
$f_{n,r}:S(n,r)\text{-mod}\to H(r)\text{-mod}$, $V\mapsto eV$, be the exact
Schur functor with left adjoint $h_{n,r}$
([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]). Let
$L_n(\lambda)$ be the irreducible $S(n,r)$-module for an $\ell$-restricted
$\lambda\vdash r$
([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]), and let
$L_n(\lambda)^1$ be its first level, the sum of the weight spaces
$L_n(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha_i}$ over the simple roots, which is naturally an
$S(n-1,r-1)$-module. Then

1. $f_{n-1,r-1}\bigl(L_n(\lambda)^1\bigr)=f_{n,r}\bigl(L_n(\lambda)\bigr)
   \bigl\downarrow_{H(r-1)}$ as $H(r-1)$-modules, naturally in the pair
   $(n,r)$;
2. for $S(n,r)$-modules $W,V$ with $W^{(e)}=W$ and $V_{(e)}=0$ one has
   $\operatorname{Hom}_{S(n,r)}(W,V)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{H(r)}(fW,fV)$,
   so the functor detects and preserves the relevant Hom spaces and, being
   exact, transfers composition multiplicities of first-level modules;
3. if $\lambda$ is $\ell$-restricted, then the socle of the restriction of
   $L_n(\lambda)^1$ to the Levi subalgebra $U(n-1)$ consists of
   $\ell$-restricted labels.

At $q=1$ (so $\ell=p$ in characteristic $p$; characteristic zero gives
$\ell=\infty$) the specialization $H(r)\to kS_r$ of
([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]])
makes (i)-(iii) statements about $kS_r$-modules and the simple $kS_{r-1}$-modules
of
[[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]].
before.strategy: Complete argument, Brundan 1998 §5.5-5.7 (complete 34-page author manuscript, pp. 30-32) and Kleshchev I §2.12(v), whose citation is replaced by this proof-bearing comparison. (i) Take the permitted stable rank $n=r$ and write the $(1^r)$-weight idempotent of $S(n,r)$; by §3.22 of the source the weight belongs to the level-1 summand, and deleting the last (level) coordinate of the weight identifies it with the $(1^{r-1})$-weight of $S(n-1,r-1)$, while the generators $T_1,\dots,T_{r-2}$ act identically before and after the deletion. Hence both sides are equal as explicit simultaneous weight spaces, naturally in $V$; this uses neither semisimplicity nor an identification of cellular and crystal labels. (ii) Is Brundan's Lemma 5.6(i)-(ii), proved by the adjunction $h\dashv f$ and the submodule $V_{(e)}$; (iii) is Lemma 5.7, whose proof uses the good-node description of the socle and shows that $i\in R^{good}(\lambda)$ implies $\lambda(i)$ is $\ell$-restricted. Composition multiplicities: apply the exact functor $f$ to a composition series of the first-level module; a surviving restricted simple maps to a Hecke simple, a killed simple contributes nothing, and by (ii) the multiplicity of a selected surviving simple is preserved. The $q=1$ specialization is the Hecke/group identification of the batch-20 item. This is the exact replacement for Kleshchev I §2.12(v) as recorded by the SYMR-9 evidence report; Step 3 must keep the weight-idempotent computation explicit.

after.title: The Schur functor compares first-level branching with Hecke restriction
after.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^\times$, $\ell=e(F,q)$, and $n\ge r\ge1$; at the empty lower-rank boundary put $S(0,0)=H(0)=F$ with its identity functor. Use the left-module version of the q-Schur algebra $S(n,r)$ and its exact Schur functor $f_{n,r}:V\mapsto eV$ with left adjoint $h_{n,r}:X\mapsto S(n,r)e\otimes_{eS(n,r)e}X$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]). Right-module suppliers are converted to left modules through their star anti-involutions. All Specht and simple labels below are **Murphy labels**: $f(W^\mu)=S_{\mathrm M}^\mu$ and $f(L_n(\mu))=D_{\mathrm M}^\mu$, the latter nonzero exactly when $\mu$ is $\ell$-restricted ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

For a degree-$r$ polynomial module $V=\bigoplus_{|\alpha|=r}V_\alpha$, its **first level** is $$V^1:=\bigoplus_{\alpha_n=1}V_\alpha.$$ It is a module for the Levi polynomial algebra $S(n-1,r-1)$: the first $n-1$ coordinates sum to $r-1$. It is not the sum of the weights one simple root below the highest weight. For an $\ell$-restricted partition $\lambda\vdash r$, the following hold.

1. There is a natural $H(r-1)$-module isomorphism $$f_{n-1,r-1}(L_n(\lambda)^1)\cong      \operatorname{Res}_{H(r-1)}^{H(r)}f_{n,r}(L_n(\lambda)).$$ 2. For any $S(n,r)$-modules $W,V$ with $W^{(e)}=W$ and $V_{(e)}=0$, the Schur functor induces $$\operatorname{Hom}_{S(n,r)}(W,V)\cong      \operatorname{Hom}_{H(r)}(fW,fV).$$ Here $W^{(e)}=S(n,r)eW$ is the intersection of submodules whose quotient is killed by $e$, and $V_{(e)}$ is the sum of submodules killed by $e$. 3. The socle of $L_n(\lambda)^1$ as a Levi module has only $\ell$-restricted labels.

For every partition $\mu\vdash r-1$ with $\mu$ $\ell$-restricted, $$[L_n(\lambda)^1:L_{n-1}(\mu)]  =[\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}:D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}].$$ The exact functor transfers these surviving multiplicities; it may kill nonrestricted simple factors. At $q=1$ these statements hold over every field for the group algebras. In ordinary James labels the dictionary is $D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}\cong D^{\lambda'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$, not an untwisted identification with $D^\lambda$ ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]]).
after.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field, parameter, ranks, polynomial weight decomposition, and q-Schur and Hecke algebras of the Statement.

[F1] The permutation-summand realization is $S(n,r)=\operatorname{End}_{H(r)}(\bigoplus_\alpha M^\alpha)$, with weight projections $1_\alpha$. The regular summand for a composition with exactly $r$ entries equal to $1$ is $M^\alpha=H(r)$. The standard corner is $\omega=(1^r,0^{n-r})$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]).

[F2] The exact Schur functor sends $W^\mu$ to $S_{\mathrm M}^\mu$ and $L_n(\mu)$ to $D_{\mathrm M}^\mu$, allowing zero images. The nonzero images have restricted labels and are pairwise nonisomorphic simple modules ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

[F3] Brundan, full author manuscript, §3.22 defines polynomial levels by last-coordinate weight, using both $K_n$ and its binomial operators so the integer weight is determined even at a root of unity. The Levi $U(n-1)$ commutes with these operators. The q-Schur polynomial realization is the corresponding finite-degree quotient. In §5.5 the functors are left-module functors; star converts the right-module suppliers to this convention.

[F4] Every Schur simple $L(\mu)$ is its nonzero cell-form quotient, so the descended symmetric associative form makes $L(\mu)^\circ\cong L(\mu)$ under Schur star. The normalized maps are $\varphi_{ST}(x_\nu h)=m_{ST}h$, with $m_{ST}\in x_\mu H\cap Hx_\nu$ and $m_{TS}=m_{ST}^*$; Schur star is $\varphi_{ST}^*=\varphi_{TS}$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). The standard coefficient trace satisfies $\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)$ and $\tau(T_u^*T_v)=\delta_{uv}q^{\ell(u)}$; its complete generator-block proof is the actual standalone trace construction of [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]. The following proof establishes the restricted-socle conclusion locally over the original field; no quantum-hyperalgebra square-root or unproved classical-specialization premise is used.

[F5] At $q=1$ the actual ordinary polytabloid/signed-conjugate Murphy comparison gives the group module dictionary, with form factor $1$, over every field. It follows through the corrected Definition and the actual NEW50 comparison and specialization suppliers, not the printed-page-25 untwisted warning ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Construct the lower-rank action directly over the given field. Put $M_0=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Lambda(n-1,r-1)}M^\alpha$ for $H(r-1)$. Length-additive parabolic coset bases give $M^{(\alpha,1)}\cong M^\alpha\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$ by $x_\alpha h\otimes a\mapsto x_\alpha ha$. Thus the summands with last coordinate $1$ form $M_1\cong M_0\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$. The functorial algebra homomorphism $f\mapsto f\otimes1$ embeds $S(n-1,r-1)$ into $\operatorname{End}_{H(r)}(M_1)$: the Hecke algebra $H(r)$ is free on its parabolic coset basis and contains the unit coset, so the map is injective. Extend these maps by zero to the remaining summands of $M$ and put $p=\sum_{\alpha_n=1}1_\alpha$. For every left $S(n,r)$-module $V$, $V^1=pV$ is therefore a natural $S(n-1,r-1)$-module. This supplies the lower-rank action without assuming that the first level is a sum of root-adjacent highest-weight spaces, and without adjoining a square root of the Hecke parameter. It agrees with the last-coordinate polynomial level of [F3]. [given, F1, F3]

1.2 Prove the Hom assertion algebraically. For $S=S(n,r)$ put $\overline W=Se\otimes_{eSe}eW$ and let $\varepsilon:\overline W\to W$ send $se\otimes w$ to $sw$. Its image is $SeW=W^{(e)}$, which is $W$ under the stated hypothesis. Applying $e$ identifies $e\varepsilon$ with the isomorphism $eSe\otimes_{eSe}eW\to eW$. Exactness of $e(-)$ therefore gives $eK=0$ for $K=\ker\varepsilon$. The exact sequence is $$0\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow\overline W   \xrightarrow{\varepsilon}W\longrightarrow0.$$ For any $S$-map $g:\overline W\to V$, its image $g(K)$ is an $S$-submodule killed by $e$, so it is contained in $V_{(e)}=0$. Thus $g$ factors uniquely through $W$. The adjunction then gives $\operatorname{Hom}_H(eW,eV)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(\overline W,V) \cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(W,V)$. This proves assertion 2, with the kernel and quotient in the correct direction. [given, F1]

2.1 Reconcile the corners for all $n\ge r$. Put $\omega_*=(1^{r-1},0^{n-r},1)$ and $e_*=1_{\omega_*}$. Both $M^\omega$ and $M^{\omega_*}$ are the regular module $H(r)$. Their fixed identity isomorphism gives block matrix units $u,v\in S(n,r)$ with $u=e_*ue$, $v=eve_*$, $uv=e_*$ and $vu=e$. Thus multiplication by $u$ gives a natural isomorphism $eV\to e_*V$, with inverse multiplication by $v$, and carries the standard regular corner action to the $e_*$ corner action. When $n=r$ these corners coincide. This explicitly supplies the natural corner identification instead of treating an idempotent with last coordinate $0$ as lying in the first level. [F1, step 1.1]

2.2 Construct a perfect Schur-contravariant form on the permutation-summand module $M$. On each distinguished coset basis $b_d=x_\alpha T_d$, put $\beta_\alpha(b_d,b_c)=\delta_{dc}q^{\ell(d)}$. The row generator cases are a same-row scalar $q$, or an adjacent length-increasing pair with $b_dT_i=b_c$ and $b_cT_i=q b_d+(q-1)b_c$, $\ell(c)=\ell(d)+1$. Their weighted diagonal matrices verify $\beta_\alpha(aT_i,b)=\beta_\alpha(a,bT_i)$, so the forms are Hecke-contravariant and perfect. To prove Schur adjointness, work first in $A=\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$. Length-additive cosets and [F4] give $\tau(a^*b)=P_\alpha(Q)\beta_\alpha(a,b)$ on $M_\alpha$, where $P_\alpha=\sum_{u\in S_\alpha}Q^{\ell(u)}$ is nonzero in $A$ with constant coefficient $1$. For $f=\varphi_{ST}:M_\nu\to M_\mu$, $a=x_\nu h$ and $b=x_\mu k$, membership in [F4] gives $m_{TS}x_\mu=P_\mu m_{TS}$ and $x_\nu m_{TS}=P_\nu m_{TS}$. Thus $$P_\mu\beta_\mu(fa,b)=\tau(h^*m_{TS}x_\mu k)=P_\mu\tau(h^*m_{TS}k),\qquad P_\nu\beta_\nu(a,f^*b)=\tau(h^*x_\nu m_{TS}k)=P_\nu\tau(h^*m_{TS}k).$$ Cancel the nonzero polynomials only in $A$, then specialize the resulting identity to $F$. The orthogonal sum $\beta=\bigoplus_\alpha\beta_\alpha$ is therefore perfect and satisfies $\beta(sm,m')=\beta(m,s^*m')$ for every actual Schur basis map and hence every $s\in S$. It identifies the left $S$-module $M$ with $M^\circ$. No Poincare factor is canceled in the given field, including at $q=1$. [F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Compute the first-level corner inside this induced action. The lower regular summand is $H(r-1)$, whose induction is $H(r-1)\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)=H(r)$, exactly the summand of type $\omega_*$. Its weight projection on $pV$ is $e_*$, so $f_{n-1,r-1}(V^1)=e_*V$. The lower corner operator given by left multiplication by $h\in H(r-1)$ induces left multiplication by the same $h$ on $H(r)$ under $a\otimes b\mapsto ab$. Thus every generator $T_1,\ldots,T_{r-2}$ acts exactly as its image in the upper regular corner, by equality of these explicit endomorphisms. The matrix units of step 2.1 identify the upper standard corner with this regular summand. They consequently give $f_{n-1,r-1}(V^1)\cong\operatorname{Res}f_{n,r}(V)$ on every module. This is an algebra-level calculation; it needs no generic semisimplicity or cellular/crystal label identification. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.2 Determine the simple socle labels of $M$. Evaluation at $1$ in the regular summand gives $Se=\operatorname{Hom}_H(H,M)\cong M$ as a left $S$-module. Finite-dimensional star duality and [F4], together with step 2.2, give $$\operatorname{Hom}_S(L,M)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(M^\circ,L^\circ)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(Se,L)\cong eL$$ for every simple $L$. The last bijection evaluates a map at $e$, with inverse $v\mapsto(se\mapsto sv)$ for $v\in eL$. By [F2], $eL(\mu)$ is nonzero exactly for restricted $\mu$. Thus every simple submodule of $M$ has restricted label; for restricted $\lambda$, any nonzero map $L(\lambda)\to M$ is injective. The proof does not equate zero form quotients with zero actual module heads. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.2, algebra]


4.1 Transfer composition multiplicities by exactness, not by a Hom-space count. Apply $f_{n-1,r-1}$ to a finite composition series of $L_n(\lambda)^1$. By [F2] its factors become either zero or the pairwise nonisomorphic $D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}$ for restricted $\mu$. Removing repeated terms of the resulting filtration therefore preserves the number of each surviving simple factor. Step 3.1 identifies its result with $\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}$, proving the stated equality. Assertion 3 is not used to claim that every composition factor survives; a socle statement alone would not justify that claim. [F2, step 3.1]

4.2 Prove the restricted-socle assertion over every original field. Applying $p$ to the injection $L_n(\lambda)\to M$ of step 3.2 embeds $L_n(\lambda)^1$ into $pM=M_1=M_0\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$ with the actual lower action of step 1.1. The length-additive parabolic coset basis makes $H(r)$ free as a LEFT $H(r-1)$-module of rank $r$, so $M_1$ is $r$ copies of $M_0$ as a left lower Schur module. Apply steps 2.2 and 3.2 to $M_0\cong S(n-1,r-1)e_{\rm lower}$: its simple socle labels are exactly the surviving restricted labels. Every simple submodule of $L_n(\lambda)^1$ is a simple submodule of $M_1$, and therefore restricted. At degree zero $M_0=F$, with the unique empty label; at $n=r=1$ this is the convention $S(0,0)=F$. This proves assertion3, without adjoining a square root, using a splitting extension, assuming a quantum-hyperalgebra specialization, or requiring $\lambda_n=0$. [F2, step 1.1, step 3.2, algebra]


5.1 At $q=1$, [F5] identifies the corner algebras with group algebras. In ordinary regular labels the two modules are simultaneously twisted by sign and both partition labels are conjugated. Sign restricts along the group tower, is exact, and preserves the two compared multiplicities. This is the ordinary group interpretation, including characteristic $2$; it is not an untwisted identification of a restricted label with the same regular label. Steps 3.1, 1.2, 4.2 and 4.1 prove all the assertions. [F5, step 3.1, step 1.2, step 4.2, step 4.1] ∎

## Remarks

The first-level and ordinary-label reconciliation above is the new authored binding repair. The previously accepted source20 cell-form repair and NEW50 ordinary polytabloid construction are unchanged. Actual acceptance requires the repaired current source20/NEW50 supplier carriers after the live writers drain and the same reviewer checks the actual bound interfaces. before.title: The complete weight-one decomposition matrix for S3 at p=3
before.statement: Take $e=p=3$ and the weight-one configuration $n=3$, $\gamma=\varnothing$ of [[thm-weight-one-block-decomposition-pattern]]; the three partitions of $3$ with $3$-core $\varnothing$ are $\lambda_1=(3)\rhd\lambda_2=(2,1)\rhd\lambda_3=(1,1,1)$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). The associated q-Schur block at $p=3$ (with $d\ge3$) has the complete Weyl/simple decomposition matrix and with rows and columns in the order $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, equal to $\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$; applying the Schur functor and the conjugation/duality dictionary gives the Murphy Specht rows $[S^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}]$, $[S^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}]+[D^{\lambda_3}_{\mathrm M}]$, $[S^{\lambda_3}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_3}_{\mathrm M}]$, which in the page's $3$-regular labels $(3),(2,1)$ is the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ with rows $(3),(2,1),(1,1,1)$ ([[thm-nakayama-block-classification-for-symmetric-groups]], [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]); the group-side entries are verified directly from the two-dimensional model $S^{(2,1)}$ of characteristic $3$, whose all-ones vector spans a trivial submodule with sign quotient, together with $S^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$ and $S^{(1,1,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$.
before.strategy: List the partitions of $3$ with $3$-core $\varnothing$: $(3)$ and $(1,1,1)$ remove their unique $3$-hook and $(2,1)$ removes its unique $3$-hook, giving exactly the three labels in the stated dominance order. Apply the weight-one theorem to obtain the bidiagonal Weyl matrix, then the Schur functor and the conjugation/duality dictionary $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^{\theta}$, $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^{\theta}$ to pass from the Murphy rows to the group-side matrix with rows and columns in the $p$-regular labels $(3),(2,1)$, and finally compare with the direct computation from the standard module: in characteristic $3$ the all-ones vector of $S^{(2,1)}$ spans a trivial submodule with sign quotient, so the rows of $S^{(3)},S^{(2,1)},S^{(1,1,1)}$ are $(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$ in the labels $(3),(2,1)$, and the simple labels are those of [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]. The two computations agree entry by entry, which is the verification of the example. No choice principle is used. Sources: Mathas, Proposition 5.38 and the accompanying discussion of $q=1$ (printed pp. 61-63); the published $S_3$ matrix.

after.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The prime $p=e=3$, the partitions $(3)$, $(2,1)$, $(1,1,1)$ of $n=3$, and the Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}_F$ of $S_F(d,3)$ for $d\ge3$ over any field $F$ of characteristic $3$, with $q=1$ and quantum characteristic $e=3$ (for example $F=\mathbb F_3$).

[F1] $3$-cores: the $3$-core of a partition is computed by removing rim $3$-hooks until none remains; $C_3((3))=\varnothing$, $C_3((2,1))=\varnothing$, $C_3((1,1,1))=\varnothing$, and these are all the partitions of $3$ with core $\varnothing$, ordered by dominance as $(3)\rhd(2,1)\rhd(1,1,1)$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]]).

[F2] The balanced positive Jantzen-submodule formula is [[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]] and its beta signs are [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. Every Weyl module has its nonzero norm-one simple head and $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$, with absolute simple heads and base-change-compatible forms ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). The specific three-row computation is proved below.

[F3] The exact integral Schur corner/form/radical identity is [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]], steps 1.1–5.1. The specific Murphy forms/actions are computed locally from the independent integral Murphy datum and row action ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]], [[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]). The signed conjugate module/form identity is [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]. No universal finite-$e$ restricted nonzero criterion is used.

[F4] Group side: the simple $k[S_3]$-modules at $p=3$ are $D^{(3)}$ and $D^{(2,1)}$, indexed by the $3$-regular partitions $(3),(2,1)$ ([[thm-nakayama-block-classification-for-symmetric-groups]], [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]).

[F5] Tabloid model: the permutation module $M^{(2,1)}_k$ over a field $k$ has the three tabloids $v_1,v_2,v_3$ as a basis, where $v_i$ is the tabloid whose singleton second row is $\{i\}$, and $\sigma\cdot v_i=v_{\sigma(i)}$; the Specht module $S^{(2,1)}_k\subseteq M^{(2,1)}_k$ has basis $e_t=v_3-v_1$ and $e_u=v_2-v_1$. Moreover $S^{(3)}_k$ is the trivial module and $S^{(1,1,1)}_k$ is the sign module ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]], [[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]).



## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The labels and their cores. The hook-length diagrams of the three partitions of $3$ are $3,2,1$ for $(3)$; $3,1$ in the first row and $1$ in the second for $(2,1)$; and $3,2,1$ vertically for $(1,1,1)$. In each case there is exactly one hook of length $3$ and removing its rim hook leaves the empty partition, so all three partitions have $3$-core $\varnothing$; conversely any partition of $3$ with core $\varnothing$ is one of these, since a partition whose core has size $3$ is its own core, and $\varnothing$ has size $0=3-3$. Dominance orders them as $(3)\rhd(2,1)\rhd(1,1,1)$. [given, F1]

2.1 Compute the Weyl matrix directly. First work over $\mathbb F_3$ with lift $R=\mathbb Z_{(3)}$, $\hat q=1$, so the only nonzero hook valuation at rank three is $v([3]_1)=1$. The conjugate beta sequence of $(3)$ is $(3,2,1)$. Its hook pairs $(3,2)$ and $(3,1)$ give the balanced sequences $(5,0,1)$ and $(4,2,0)$, of sorted shapes $(1,1,1)$ with sign $-1$ and $(2,1)$ with sign $+1$, respectively. The other pair has coefficient zero. Thus its positive sum is $[W^{(2,1)}]-[W^{(1,1,1)}]$. For $(2,1)$, beta $(4,2,0)$ and its only nonzero pair $(3,1)$ give $(5,1,0)$, shape $(1,1,1)$ with sign $+1$, so its positive sum is $[W^{(1,1,1)}]$. The column shape has no row pair and zero positive sum, hence $W^{(1,1,1)}=L^{(1,1,1)}$. Positivity and $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$ then show that $W^{(2,1)}(1)=L^{(1,1,1)}$ and every higher submodule is zero, giving $[W^{(2,1)}]=[L^{(2,1)}]+[L^{(1,1,1)}]$. Substitute into the first sum to get $[L^{(2,1)}]$; the same argument gives $[W^{(3)}]=[L^{(3)}]+[L^{(2,1)}]$. This proves exactly the displayed complete Weyl matrix. Scalar extension to any original field $F$ of characteristic three preserves the Weyl modules/forms and the composition series, since all Schur simple heads are absolutely simple by [F2]. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Determine the specific corner images directly. The group row symmetrizer $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}w$ satisfies $x_{(3)}^2=6x_{(3)}$, so its rank-one Murphy form is zero in characteristic three. In the rank-one column cell the generator is $1$ and its square coefficient is $1$; the higher ideal contains $1+T_1$ and $1+T_2$ (the latter is a conjugate of the former), so this cell and its nonzero form quotient are the sign module. For the middle cell put $x=1+T_1$, $c_0=x$ and $c_1=xT_2$ modulo the higher row ideal. Its row symmetrizer satisfies $x_{(3)}=x+xT_2+xT_2T_1$, so $c_1T_1=-c_0-c_1$ while $c_0T_1=c_0$; and $T_2^2=1$ gives $c_0T_2=c_1$, $c_1T_2=c_0$. Thus its generator matrices are $M_1=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\-1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $M_2=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The independent cell products $x^2=2x$, $xT_2x=x_{(3)}-x\equiv-x$ and $xT_2^2x=2x$ give $G=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ over $F$. Its radical is the line $(1,-1)$; modulo it both generators act by $1$, so $D_{\mathrm M}^{(2,1)}$ is the nonzero trivial module. These two simple images are distinct since $1\ne-1$. The exact corner/form identity [F3] therefore kills precisely $L^{(3)}$ among the three labels. Projecting the Weyl matrix just proved gives all displayed Murphy Specht rows over the original $F$, without any general finite-$e$ nonzero-label criterion. [F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Dipper-James rows and the direct group computation. Conjugating the partitions $(3)\leftrightarrow(1,1,1)$, $(2,1)\leftrightarrow(2,1)$ and applying the signed $\theta$-pullback to every Hecke module, the rows of step 3.1 become $[S^{(1,1,1)}]=[D^{(2,1)}]$, $[S^{(2,1)}]=[D^{(2,1)}]+[D^{(3)}]$ and $[S^{(3)}]=[D^{(3)}]$ in the $3$-regular labels, that is, the matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with rows $(3),(2,1),(1,1,1)$ and columns $(3),(2,1)$. For the independent direct check, put $w:=e_t+e_u=v_3-v_1+v_2-v_1=v_1+v_2+v_3$ in characteristic $3$: then $w\ne0$ spans a one-dimensional submodule, since $\sigma\cdot v_i=v_{\sigma(i)}$ gives $\sigma\cdot w=w$ for every $\sigma\in S_3$, so it realises the trivial module; and in the quotient, $(12)\cdot e_t+e_t=(v_3-v_2)+(v_3-v_1)=2v_3-v_1-v_2=3v_3-w\equiv0$ shows that $(12)$ acts by $-1$, so the quotient is the sign module. With $S^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$, $S^{(1,1,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$ by [F5], and $D^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$, $D^{(2,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$ by [F4], the direct rows of $S^{(3)},S^{(2,1)},S^{(1,1,1)}$ are $(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$, matching the matrix obtained from the Schur functor entry by entry. [F4, F5, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
